prime.problem: The source guide is 181 cards' worth of terse interview notes spread over ten courses. Without a map you read it in file order, hit a card that assumes heaps or SLO arithmetic you haven't met, and can't tell which third of it your next interview actually tests.
prime.fits: This is the series map, read before cs-1 or after the last course as a recap. It builds on nothing; every later course is one box on it, and each box's arrows are the Needs column from the series index.
expect: four independent tracks (coding, large-scale design, OS, research engineering)
the Needs arrows as a dependency graph
how each card is built (definition → example → 2×2 → clarification → Python)
where each source page went, and which cards were written from references
prime.goal: Draw the ten courses as a dependency graph from memory, pick a valid reading order for a given interview, and say which cards rest on the source guide and which on outside references.

attend: Which three courses have no incoming arrows, besides cs-1, and what does that mean for where you can start?
cs-6 lists cs-2's sorting as something that helps, not something it needs. What would change on the map if that became a hard arrow?
Why does cs-7 stand alone in its column, and why does the card still tell design candidates to read it beside cs-4 to cs-6?
cs-10 needs both cs-8 and cs-9. Which ideas travel along each of those two arrows?
49 cards were written from references rather than the source. Why does the card say so in every such footer instead of blending them in?

must: Each course lists only the courses it truly needs → the Needs arrows form a small graph with no cycles → any order that respects the arrows is valid (a topological order) → you can start a track at any course with no arrows in (cs-1, cs-4, cs-7, cs-8)

The four tracks share no hard arrows → studying one never blocks on another → an interview picks a track (coding → cs-1→2→3, design → cs-4→5→6, quant → cs-8→9→10) → cross-track links are only "also skim" suggestions

The source has empty headings (all of OS, all of financial maths, 24 scattered cards) → those cards are written from standard references → the footer says so → you know which claims come from the source guide and which from the series, which is what makes the corrections card possible

Every card follows one build (definition → worked example with real numbers → 2×2 of losers vs winner → when it doesn't apply → runnable Python) → you know where on any card to find the mechanism, the tradeoff and the limit → you can skim a course fast and retrieve from the same slots
elevated: Timings come from one Apple M3 in Python → absolute numbers won't match your machine → compare ratios between variants on a card, not raw milliseconds
reference: which source page maps to which course (the "Where each part of the source went" table)
the three starter cards listed per interview
Python 3.10 and the code/ folder per course

compress.prompt: Course-level compress: without looking, draw the whole series as one graph. Ten boxes in four columns, the Needs arrows between them, the dashed "helps" links, and a label on each track for the interview it serves. Then write one sentence on why any arrow-respecting order works.
checklist: coding: cs-1 → cs-2 → cs-3 (cs-1's heaps help cs-3's Dijkstra)
design: cs-4 → cs-5 → cs-6 (cs-2's sorting helps cs-6's MapReduce)
OS: cs-7 alone, read beside the design track
research: cs-8 → cs-9 → cs-10, plus cs-8 → cs-10 directly
no arrows between tracks, so the graph has four components and many valid orders
which courses are written wholly from references (cs-7, cs-10)

retrieve.q: Explain to a friend starting interview prep why the series can say "read anytime" about some courses but insists on order within a track.
answer: the Needs arrows only exist inside tracks
a course with no incoming arrow (cs-1, cs-4, cs-7, cs-8) can be read first
inside a track each course uses the previous one's tools: Big-O and heaps, requirements and SLO arithmetic, MGFs and conditioning
cross-track links are "helps", never "needs"

retrieve.q: Walk through how you'd turn "I have a quant interview and a system design interview" into one reading order using only the map.
answer: pick the two tracks: cs-4 → cs-5 → cs-6 and cs-8 → cs-9 → cs-10
the tracks are independent, so interleave them or read one then the other
within each, respect the arrows (cs-10 last, after both cs-8 and cs-9)
optionally add cs-7 beside the design track; total 53 + 47 = 100 cards, or 113 with cs-7

retrieve.q: You have one week before a coding round and can't read all 68 coding cards. What does the map suggest you give up, and what does that cost you?
answer: start from the three starter cards (testing, binary search on the answer, recursion to DP) instead of reading in order
skip whole groups rather than skimming everything
the cost: later cards assume earlier tools, so a skipped prerequisite shows up as a card you can't follow
each card's "Needs first" line tells you which gap to repair

retrieve.q: Which parts of the series would you trust least if the source guide were your only reference, and how does the map tell you?
answer: cards written from references (all of cs-7 and cs-10, plus 24 others) have no source content to check against
their footers say the heading was empty
the source-derived cards are checked against the source, and its errors listed on the corrections card

compare.q: The map's reading orders vs Kahn's algorithm on course prerequisites: what is the map's Needs column in that card's terms, and what would a cycle in it mean for a reader?
answer: each course is a node; each Needs entry is an edge that must point forward
a valid reading order is a topological order; cs-1, cs-4, cs-7 and cs-8 start with in-degree 0
many orders are valid because the four tracks are separate components
a cycle (A needs B, B needs A) would leave both stuck with in-degree 1: no valid order, so neither could be read first

compare.q: This card maps where each part of the source went; the corrections card audits how right each part was. Which question does each answer, and why do you need the map before reading the audit?
answer: map: which course covers a topic and what to read first
audit: which cards fix a source error and how it was checked
the audit is grouped by course, so it reads as a tour of the map
the map's supplemented-card count explains why cs-7 and cs-10 have no rows in the audit

compare.q: The series map vs a single course's overview: what does each organise by, and when would you open one rather than the other?
answer: the series map organises courses by track and prerequisite
a course overview organises one course's cards by the decision they support (for cs-1: which structure to reach for and what each one costs)
open the map to choose what to study; open a course overview to choose which card answers a problem in front of you

predict.q: Suppose cs-6 turned cs-2's sorting from "helps" into a hard Need. Before counting: how many cards would a reader have to finish before opening cs-6, compared with today, and what happens to the claim that the four tracks are independent?
predict.answer: Today cs-6 needs only cs-4 and cs-5: 16 + 20 = 36 cards. With a hard arrow from cs-2 it also needs cs-2 and, through it, cs-1: 36 + 20 + 21 = 77 cards, more than double. The coding and design tracks would join into one component, so a design-only candidate could no longer skip the coding track.

apply.task: Plan a 12-week study schedule for a candidate with a system design round and a quant round, at about 10 cards a week. Use the map's counts and arrows: list the courses in a valid order, total the cards, decide whether cs-7 fits, and name the first card you'd open in each track.
apply.done: Your order respects every Needs arrow (cs-4 before cs-5 before cs-6; cs-8 before cs-9 before cs-10); design plus quant is 53 + 47 = 100 cards (10 weeks), and adding cs-7 makes 113 (about 11.3 weeks), which still fits in 12.
apply.hint: The two tracks share no arrows, so alternating a design week and a quant week is as valid as finishing one track first.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: how many cards sit before cs-6, or whether the tracks would stay independent?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why cs-10 needs cs-8 directly as well as through cs-9?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: source page → course, or course → interview?
Which track will you start, and which of its courses has no incoming arrow?
Revisit this card after your first course: can you redraw the graph without looking?
